narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The three factors that mattered most to this decision were your undergraduate grades in law school, your performance in the third year of studies, and your family income level. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) in your third year, compared with an average around the middle of the class (5.8) among accepted students, signaled to the model that you might struggle with the demands of legal study and the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.60 actually worked in your favor. It is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward passing. Similarly, coming from a low-income family also nudged the outcome slightly toward success, since very few low-income students appear in the accepted group and the model treats this as a modest positive factor.

Even with these helpful elements, your low third-year ranking outweighed them. The final prediction crossed the line into likely failure, so the admission decision went against you.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record in any remaining coursework, consider retaking key classes to improve your ranking, and explore bar-preparation programs designed for students with similar profiles. These steps can meaningfully change your prospects for future applications. (248 words)
